topics.title: 1.1 Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension

outcomes.text: Describe a scalar or vector quantity using magnitude and direction as appropriate
Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction
Draw vectors as arrows whose length is proportional to magnitude
Classify distance and speed as scalars, and position, displacement, velocity, acceleration as vectors; use vector notation and signs in one dimension
Describe a vector sum in one dimension
In a one-dimensional coordinate system, opposite directions carry opposite signs when adding vectors
Describe a change in an object's position
Treat an object as a single point when its size, shape and internal makeup can be ignored
Define displacement as the change in position

subtopics.title: Average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration

outcomes.text: Describe the average velocity and acceleration of an object
Calculate averages from the initial and final states over a time interval
Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time
Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by elapsed time
An object accelerates when the magnitude or direction of its velocity changes
Over very small intervals, averages approach instantaneous velocity and acceleration
Describe position, velocity and acceleration using representations of motion
Represent motion with diagrams, graphs, equations and narrative descriptions
Apply the three constant-acceleration kinematic equations in one dimension
Near Earth's surface, gravity gives a constant downward acceleration of about 10 m/s squared
Use slopes and areas of position, velocity and acceleration graphs to relate the quantities
Describe the reference frame of a given observer
The chosen reference frame sets the direction and size of measured quantities
Describe motion as measured by observers in different inertial frames
Convert measurements between reference frames
Observed velocity combines the object's velocity with the observer frame's velocity by vector addition; acceleration is the same in all inertial frames

topics.title: 1.5 Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions

outcomes.text: Describe the perpendicular components of a vector
Model a vector as the resultant of two perpendicular components
Resolve vectors into components along a chosen coordinate system
Use trigonometry and the Pythagorean theorem to find components
Describe the motion of an object moving in two dimensions
Analyse 2D motion by splitting it into components and using 1D kinematics
Projectile motion has zero acceleration in one dimension and constant nonzero acceleration in the other
Describe the properties and interactions of a system
System properties come from the interactions of objects inside it
A system can be treated as one object when its internal details do not matter
Systems can exchange energy or mass with the environment
Individual objects in a system may behave differently from the system as a whole
The internal structure of a system affects how it must be analysed
Changing external variables can change a system's substructure
Describe the location of a system's center of mass relative to its parts
For symmetric mass distributions the center of mass lies on lines of symmetry
Calculate the center of mass along an axis for a few particles
Model a system as a single object at its center of mass
Describe a force as an interaction between two objects or systems
Forces are vectors from interactions; an object cannot exert a net force on itself
Contact forces are macroscopic effects of electric forces between atoms
Describe the forces on an object using a free-body diagram
Free-body diagrams help visualise forces and write equations
Show every environmental force on the object
Draw forces as vectors starting from the center of mass dot
Choose an axis parallel to the acceleration to simplify the algebra
Describe an interaction using Newton's third law and paired forces
The two objects in an interaction exert equal and opposite forces on each other
Internal forces do not change the motion of a system's center of mass
Tension is the net result of forces between segments of a string under external force
Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity stays constant
Net force is the vector sum of all forces on the system
Translational equilibrium means the net force is zero
With zero net force, velocity stays constant (Newton's first law)
Forces balanced in one dimension may be unbalanced in another
An inertial frame is one where Newton's first law holds
Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity changes
Unbalanced forces mean a nonzero net force
Acceleration is proportional to net force and in the same direction (Newton's second law)
Velocity of the center of mass changes only with a nonzero net external force
Describe the gravitational interaction between two objects with mass
Gravitational force is proportional to both masses and inversely to distance squared; attractive, along the line of centers
A field models a noncontact force; gravitational field strength is force per unit mass
Weight is the gravitational force from an astronomical body on a small nearby object
Describe when the gravitational force can be treated as constant
Gravity is constant when it barely changes over the displacement
Near Earth's surface, g is about 10 N/kg
Describe when apparent weight differs from the gravitational force
Apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force on the system
In an accelerating system, apparent weight differs from gravitational force
A system appears weightless when gravity is the only force on it
The equivalence principle: an observer in a noninertial frame cannot tell apparent weight from gravity
Describe inertial and gravitational mass
Inertial mass measures resistance to changes in motion
Gravitational mass relates to the gravitational attraction between systems
Inertial and gravitational mass have been experimentally found to be equal
Describe kinetic friction between two surfaces
Kinetic friction acts when surfaces slide, opposing relative motion and independent of contact area
Kinetic friction equals the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force; the normal force is perpendicular to the surface
Describe static friction between two surfaces
Static friction can act between surfaces not moving relative to each other
Static friction adjusts to prevent slipping, up to a maximum value
The static coefficient is typically greater than the kinetic coefficient
Describe the force exerted on an object by an ideal spring
An ideal spring is massless and exerts force proportional to its change in length
The spring force magnitude follows Hooke's law
The spring force always points toward the equilibrium position
Describe the motion of an object traveling in a circular path
Centripetal acceleration points to the center with magnitude v squared over r
Centripetal acceleration comes from one or more forces or force components, such as at the top of a loop, banked curves and conical pendulums
Tangential acceleration is the rate of change of speed, tangent to the path
Net acceleration is the vector sum of centripetal and tangential parts
Describe uniform circular motion with period and frequency
Describe circular orbits using Kepler's third law
In circular orbit, gravity alone provides the centripetal acceleration, relating period and radius to the central mass
Describe the translational kinetic energy of an object from its mass and velocity
Kinetic energy equals one half mass times speed squared
Kinetic energy is a scalar
Observers in different reference frames measure different kinetic energies
Describe the work done on an object or system by a force or collection of forces
Work is energy transferred into or out of a system by a force acting over a distance; conservative work is path independent, nonconservative work is not
Work is a scalar that can be positive, negative or zero
Work by a constant force depends on the force component parallel to the displacement
Net work equals the change in kinetic energy (work-energy theorem), and friction dissipates energy equal to friction force times path length
Work equals the area under a force versus displacement graph
Describe the potential energy of a system
A system has potential energy when its objects interact only through conservative forces
Potential energy is a scalar tied to the positions of objects in the system
The zero of potential energy is chosen by the observer for convenience
Use elastic, general gravitational and near-surface gravitational potential energy formulas
Total potential energy of many objects is the sum over pairs
Describe the energies present in a system
A single-object system can have only kinetic energy
Systems with conservative interactions or reversible shape changes can have kinetic and potential energy
Describe a system's behavior using conservation of mechanical energy
Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential energy
A change in one energy type is balanced by changes in others or by transfer with the surroundings
A system can be chosen so its total energy is constant
A change in total energy equals the energy transferred in or out
Describe how choosing the system determines whether its energy changes
Energy is conserved in all interactions
With zero work and no nonconservative interactions, mechanical energy is constant
Nonzero work means energy moves between system and environment
Describe energy transfer into, out of or within a system in terms of power
Power is the rate of energy change over time
Average power is energy transferred divided by time
Average power equals total work divided by time
Instantaneous power from a constant force equals force component along velocity times speed
Describe the linear momentum of an object or system
Momentum equals mass times velocity
Momentum is a vector in the direction of velocity
Use momentum to analyse collisions and explosions, using the object model for the initial and final states
Describe the impulse delivered to an object or system
Net external force is the rate of change of momentum
Impulse is average force times the time it acts
Impulse is a vector along the net force
Impulse equals the area under a force versus time graph
Net force equals the slope of a momentum versus time graph
Relate the impulse on a system to its change in momentum
Change in momentum is final minus initial momentum
Impulse equals change in momentum (impulse-momentum theorem)
Newton's second law follows from the impulse-momentum theorem for constant mass
Describe a system's behavior using conservation of linear momentum
A collection of objects has one center-of-mass velocity, constant with no net external force
Total momentum is the sum of the parts' momenta
Without external forces, momentum changes inside a system cancel; changes in system momentum equal the impulse from outside
Apply conservation of momentum to find velocities just before and after collisions or explosions
Describe how choosing the system determines whether its momentum changes
Momentum is conserved in all interactions
With zero net external force, total momentum is constant
With nonzero net external force, momentum is exchanged with the environment
Describe whether an interaction between objects is elastic or inelastic
Elastic collisions keep total kinetic energy the same
In an elastic collision individual kinetic energies may still change
Inelastic collisions lose total kinetic energy
Lost kinetic energy is converted by nonconservative forces into other forms
In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick together
Describe rotation over time using angular displacement, velocity and acceleration
Angular displacement is the angle in radians a point on a rigid system turns through about an axis; pick clockwise or counterclockwise as positive
Average angular velocity is the rate of change of angular position
Average angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity
Rotational quantities and equations mirror linear kinematics, including constant-acceleration equations and graphs
Link the linear motion of a point on a rotating rigid system to its rotational motion
Arc length equals radius times angle
Relate linear velocity and tangential acceleration to angular velocity and acceleration
All points of a rigid system share the same angular velocity and acceleration
Identify the torques exerted on a rigid system
Only the force component perpendicular to the position vector produces torque
The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action
Describe the torques exerted on a rigid system
Use force diagrams that show where forces act relative to the axis
Torque magnitude depends on force, distance from axis and the angle between them
Describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system about an axis
Rotational inertia resists changes in rotation and depends on mass and its distance from the axis
A point mass has rotational inertia mass times radius squared
Total rotational inertia is the sum over the objects
Describe rotational inertia about an axis not through the center of mass
Rotational inertia is smallest when the axis passes through the center of mass
Use the parallel axis theorem for axes parallel to one through the center of mass

topics.title: 5.5 Rotational Equilibrium and Newton's First Law in Rotational Form

outcomes.text: Describe when a system's angular velocity stays constant
Rotational and translational equilibrium can occur independently; rotational equilibrium means zero net torque and constant angular velocity
Unbalanced torques must change angular velocity

topics.title: 5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

outcomes.text: Describe when a system's angular velocity changes
Angular velocity changes when net torque is nonzero
Angular acceleration is proportional to net torque and inversely proportional to rotational inertia
Analyse linear and rotational motion separately for a full description

units.title: Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

outcomes.text: Describe the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid system from its rotational inertia and angular velocity
Rotational kinetic energy is half rotational inertia times angular velocity squared; total kinetic energy adds the translational part
A rigid system can have rotational kinetic energy while its center of mass is at rest
Rotational kinetic energy is a scalar
Describe the work done on a rigid system by a torque
A torque transfers energy when exerted through an angular displacement
Work depends on torque magnitude and angular displacement
Work equals the area under a torque versus angular position graph
Describe the angular momentum of an object or rigid system
Angular momentum of a rigid system is rotational inertia times angular velocity
Angular momentum of an object about a point depends on the chosen axis or point, mass, speed and angle
Describe the angular impulse delivered by a torque
Angular impulse is torque times the time it acts
Angular impulse points in the direction of the torque
Angular impulse equals the area under a torque versus time graph
Relate change in angular momentum to angular impulse
Compare final and initial angular momentum to find the change
Angular impulse equals change in angular momentum, a result of the rotational second law
Net torque is the slope of an angular momentum versus time graph
Angular impulse equals the area under a net torque versus time graph
Describe a system's behavior using conservation of angular momentum
Total angular momentum is the sum over the parts about the same axis
Changes in angular momentum come from interaction with the surroundings; a nonrigid system can change spin by moving mass toward or away from the axis
Describe how choosing the system determines whether its angular momentum changes
Angular momentum is conserved in all interactions
Zero net external torque means constant angular momentum
Nonzero net external torque transfers angular momentum to or from the environment
Describe the kinetic energy of a system with translation and rotation
Total kinetic energy is translational plus rotational
Describe a system rolling without slipping
Link center-of-mass speed and acceleration to angular speed and acceleration through the radius
In ideal rolling without slipping, friction dissipates no energy
Describe a system that rolls while slipping
When slipping, center-of-mass motion and rotation cannot be directly related
Kinetic friction at a slipping contact dissipates energy
Describe the motion of two objects interacting only by gravity
The motion of a massive central object is negligible next to a light satellite

Conservation laws constrain orbits: circular orbits keep energy and angular momentum constant; elliptical orbits change speed and potential energy; gravitational potential energy is zero at infinite distance
Escape velocity gives zero total mechanical energy and can be derived from energy conservation
Describe simple harmonic motion
SHM is a special case of periodic motion
SHM occurs when the restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium; small-angle pendulums qualify
Describe the frequency and period of an object in SHM
Period is the inverse of frequency; know the period formulas for a spring oscillator and a small-angle pendulum

subtopics.title: Displacement, velocity and acceleration in SHM

outcomes.text: Describe displacement, velocity and acceleration of an object in SHM
Displacement follows a cosine or sine of time; know where velocity and acceleration peak or vanish
Changing amplitude does not change period
Analyse SHM properties from graphs
Describe the mechanical energy of a system in SHM
Total energy is kinetic plus potential
Total energy in SHM is constant
Kinetic energy is greatest where potential energy is least
Potential energy is greatest where kinetic energy is zero; amplitude sets the total energy
Describe the properties of a fluid
Solids, liquids and gases differ by how their atoms and molecules interact
A fluid has no fixed shape
Density is mass per unit volume
An ideal fluid is incompressible and has no viscosity
Describe the pressure from a force on a surface
Pressure is perpendicular force per unit area
Pressure is a scalar
An incompressible fluid keeps constant volume and density under pressure
Describe the pressure exerted by a fluid
Fluid pressure comes from particle interactions with the surface
Absolute pressure is reference (such as atmospheric) plus gauge pressure
Gauge pressure of a vertical fluid column depends on density, g and depth
Describe when a fluid's velocity changes
Newton's laws describe motion of particles in a fluid
Fluid behaviour results from internal interactions and external forces
Describe the buoyant force on an object in a fluid
Buoyant force is a net upward force from the fluid
It results from the collective forces of fluid particles on the object
Its size equals the weight of displaced fluid
Describe incompressible flow through a cross-section using mass conservation
A pressure difference drives flow; flow rate depends on cross-sectional area and speed
The continuity equation says area times speed is constant
Describe flow resulting from an energy difference in the fluid-Earth system
Height differences produce differences in kinetic energy and pressure by conservation laws
Bernoulli's equation expresses conservation of mechanical energy in flow
Torricelli's theorem gives exit speed from the height of the fluid surface above the opening
